definition: Word error rate (WER) is a common metric of the performance of a speech recognition or machine translation system.
details: The WER metric typically ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates that the compared pieces of text are exactly identical, and 1 (or larger) indicates that they are completely different with no similarity. This way, a WER of 0.8 means that there is an 80% error rate for compared sentences. The general difficulty of measuring performance lies in the fact that the recognized word sequence can have a different length from the reference word sequence (supposedly the correct one). The WER is derived from the Levenshtein distance, working at the word level instead of the phoneme level. The WER is a valuable tool for comparing different systems as well as for evaluating improvements within one system. This kind of measurement, however, provides no details on the nature of translation errors and further work is therefore required to identify the main source(s) of error and to focus any research effort. This problem is solved by first aligning the recognized word sequence with the reference (spoken) word sequence using dynamic string alignment. Examination of this issue is seen through a theory called the power law that states the correlation between perplexity and word error rate. Word error r

explainer.lead: Word error rate is the standard yardstick for speech recognition and machine translation output. It matters because it converts alignment differences between a hypothesis and a reference into a single comparable number.

tiers.eli5: You read out a sentence, the computer writes down what it heard, and we count the words it got wrong compared with the right transcript.
tiers.practitioner: Teams report WER to compare ASR or MT systems and to track progress; a pitfall is ignoring normalization choices and length mismatches, since the recognized sequence can differ in length from the reference.
tiers.paperLevel: WER is derived from the alignment between recognized and reference word sequences, usually as the number of substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by the number of reference words; it ranges from 0 for identical text to 1 or more for completely different text, so 0.8 means an 80% error rate.

explainer.example: A reference of ten words compared against a hypothesis with three substituted words scores roughly 3/10 = 0.3 WER, or a 30% error rate.
